identity.title: Mobile group II intron reverse transcriptases: evolution, biochemical activities, and applications.

content.abstract: Bacterial mobile group II intron-encoded reverse transcriptases are structurally similar to an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and may have evolved at the time of transition from an RNA to DNA world. Mobile group II intron reverse transcriptases remain prevalent in bacteria, where they diversified into different subtypes, as well as into chromosomally encoded reverse transcriptases that acquired a variety of cellular functions, including phage defense, RNA spacer acquisition in CRISPR systems, and host cell DNA double-strand break and oxidative DNA damage repair. Mobile group II intron and related reverse transcriptases have remarkably beneficial biochemical properties for biotechnological applications, including high-throughput RNA sequencing. Thermostable Group II Intron-encoded Reverse Transcriptases from bacterial thermophiles, the first of these enzymes shown to have such properties, were used to develop a comprehensive RNA sequencing method that enables simultaneous profiling of virtually all RNA biotypes in human cells, extracellular vesicles, and plasma. In recent studies, Thermostable Group II Intron Reverse Transcriptase sequencing identified a novel large class of short (<300 nt) largely structured Full-Length EXcised linear Intron RNAs in human cells and plasma; enabled parallel analysis of transcriptional and post-transcriptional gene regulation by mapping Thermostable Group II Intron Reverse Transcriptase sequencing reads to genome and transcriptome reference sequences and calculating intron/exon depth ratios; and detected numerous differentially expressed RNAs in inflammatory breast cancer patient tumors and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Differentially expressed RNAs with high intron/exon depth ratios in inflammatory breast cancer patient tumors and peripheral blood mononuclear cells were correlated with pre-mRNA and intron RNA fragments detected in plasma and included the first potential inflammatory breast cancer biomarkers.
